title: Chapter 73 – The Sample
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

Feng is waiting at the courtyard gate that night, with a covered lantern.

Jian sees the small yellow glow from the end of the lane and knows the limp before he knows the shape. His brother stands very straight against the wall, in a gray tunic gone soft at the cuffs, with the lantern held low so it does not light his face. He has the look he wore at the Garden's gate on the night of the siege: a young man holding his ground against something he has not named.

"You are late," says Feng.

"The steward kept me."

"I know. I asked." Feng falls into step beside him, down the lane toward the wall. The path runs between pine trees and a row of dark outbuildings. A watchman's gong sounds somewhere far below. "Healer Song cut my dose. The Hall of Enforcement has been asking him questions. He says he is under no obligation to answer them."

"Is he?"

"He is under every obligation. He has a very smooth face." A short breath that is almost a laugh. "I have come to say two things. One of them is not about me."

Jian waits.

"The lock hummed again," says Feng. "Two nights ago, third watch. I was on the stair for a night duty. It is a duty I am allowed, because I am the first-ranker, and because no one else wants it." The lantern swings. "It hummed twice. Not once. Twice, a breath apart, and the second time it was lower."

Twice. Jian has no way to know what that means. He tells himself so, and something small and cold turns over in his chest.

"It has never hummed twice," says Feng. "Not in the six years I have been climbing it. The keepers think it is the array settling. The old one, Keeper Fu, says it is the wind in the plate." He stops under a pine. "I do not think it is the wind."

"What do you think?"

"I think it is waiting for something." Feng's voice is quite steady. "And I think you know what."

The lantern lights his jaw from below. He is twenty-six. He is the best disciple the Outer Court has produced in a generation, and he has just asked his twenty-year-old brother a question that he knows the boy will not answer.

"I do not know what it is, Feng."

"No." Feng holds his gaze. "That is a true answer. It is the true half. I will take it." He looks away, up through the trees at the dark shape of the mountain. "I told you at the Register that you should say it is a pill. Do you remember?"

"Yes."

"If anyone asks what you are doing at the Pill Hall, say it. If anyone asks what you are looking at, on the stairs, say it. Say it is a pill. Say it until they are bored." A thin smile. "It is a good lie because it is nearly true."

"Feng."

"What?"

"Thank you."

"For what?" Feng is already turning. "For being born second? Go to bed. The gong is at the fifth hour." He lifts the lantern. Then, over his shoulder, in a tone so casual that it takes Jian a moment to hear it: "I paid your meals for this week. Do not argue."

"I have eighty points."

"You have eighty points and no stones, and a ledger I am told you keep on the underside of a cot." The light goes up the lane. "A boy who counts is a boy who is short. Go to bed."

Jian watches the lantern until it turns the corner. Then he stands for a moment longer in the dark with his hands in his sleeves.

He knows I took something. He does not know what. He guesses it matters, and he lets me keep it.

It is not the first debt he has owed his brother, and he has begun to think it will not be the last.

* * *

The first thing Jian learns in the Pill Hall is how to count wrong.

He does it at furnace fourteen, at the hour after dawn, with the whole courtyard watching and nobody appearing to. The flame is low and red. He has tonight's herbs in a row on the bench: moonroot, red bark, dew-lily, stone-salt. He lifts the lid, drops in the moonroot, and begins to count aloud, in the flat singsong the Hall teaches.

"One. Two. Three."

He does not look at the numbers. He looks at the flame. At the edge of the kettle the red is going to amber, and he knows that in about forty breaths the root will be ready, and he goes on counting as though he had sixty.

"Forty-one. Forty-two."

"You are rushing," says a voice at his shoulder.

It belongs to a girl with ink on her fingers. Her name is Hua Ning, and she is fifteen, and she has been an apprentice of the Hall for three years without once being allowed to light a furnace on her own. She stands with her arms folded and a look of faint, steady dislike.

"The scroll says sixty."

"Yes, Senior Sister."

"You are at forty-four."

"I lost count," says Jian, mildly. "I will begin again."

He does not begin again. He lifts the root at forty-four, because the flame says so, and sets it on the stone, and it is brown. Hua Ning's eyes drop to it. Her mouth tightens. Behind her, Steward Gu has found something absorbing to do with a jar.

"Luck," she says.

"Yes, Senior Sister."

"You will not be lucky forever."

"No."

She goes. He finishes the batch, counting loudly, wrongly, in the wrong places, and he does it with a care that costs him more than the alchemy. To count right is to be a boy who follows the scroll. To count wrong, but wrong in a way that happens to land right, is to be a boy who is lucky. Luck is forgiven. Skill is remembered.

An advantage hidden is an advantage that must be paid for in small things every day.

He has begun to feel the weight of that. It is not heavy. It is only constant, like a stone in a shoe.

* * *

Twelve apprentices stand in a half circle in the furnace room, and Jian is the only one who does not want to be at the front.

It is the sixth day of his trial. The charcoal has been banked since dawn. Elder Bai sits on his low stool beside the bronze furnace with a bowl of plums in his lap, and on the stone ring beside him, under a dome of clear jade the size of a cooking pot, rests the red lacquer box.

The lid is open. The pill lies in its bed of black silk. Nobody has said what it is.

"A lecture," says Bai, "is a rare thing in this Hall. I give one when a matter cannot be written down. This is one of those matters." He eats a plum. "Come closer. Not you, Gu. You have seen it. The boy at the end. Yes. Lin Jian. Stand by the dome."

Eleven heads turn. Eleven pairs of eyes, most of them younger than he is by five or six years, measure the new apprentice with the flat appraising look of people who have waited a long time for a place and watched a late-comer walk into it.

Jian steps up to the stone ring. He folds his hands in front of him. The dome is warm. The pill, under it, hums.

He is doing this on purpose.

He knows it at once. Three days ago, in this room, the Elder said: I would rather you looked in my presence than in my absence. He has not been left alone with the box since. And now, in front of the whole Hall, in the clear light of a morning lecture, he has been placed at arm's length from it.

It is a test. Or an offer. Perhaps, with this man, they are the same thing.

* * *

"Level 2," says Bai, to the room. "Foundation Establishment. What does the name tell you?"

"It makes Foundation, Elder," says a young man with a long jaw.

"It does not make Foundation. Nothing makes Foundation. The disciple makes Foundation, over three days, by building a platform out of his own Qi, flesh and soul. The pill is a scaffold." He holds up a thick finger. "What does a scaffold do?"

Silence.

"It holds the walls while the mortar dries. It is thrown away afterward." Bai eats a plum. "A pill of the destination realm may do what no other pill may: it may be stronger than the body that swallows it. All other pills must match their consumer. A Level 2 pill taken by a Qi Refining disciple would be a hammer swung at an egg. But at the moment of breakthrough, when the walls are open and the body is asking for more than it can hold, the destination pill may exceed it. That is the whole law. Who can tell me why?"

Hua Ning says, "Because the realm is about to change."

"Because the realm is about to change." The Elder nods. "The old walls fall. The new walls have not been poured. In that moment the body can hold what it could not hold before, and for the length of three days, the pill does the work of a hundred years." He taps the dome. "This one has not yet done its work. It has waited six hundred years. Look at it."

They look.

And Jian, who has stood at this ring for the length of a full minute with his hands folded and his face still, makes the decision he has been refusing to make for three days.

I will never have a better chance. He has put me here.

He has thirty-seven points of cultivation energy. The Scan Structure of an object of this grade, he has estimated, will cost about thirty. That would leave him seven. After the Reboot there will be nothing, but the Reboot is a month away and a gamble in itself, and a formula in hand is worth more than a handful of spare energy.

Even so.

The cost is not only the energy. It is exposure. A Scan Structure draws, for the length of a breath, a faint cold spiral of light behind his eyes. No one has ever seen it. But no one has ever stood at an arm's length from a Foundation alchemist while it happened.

He gazes at the pill. He lets his eyes rest on it, empty, unfocused, in the manner of a boy who has been told to look at something and is trying to look attentive.

Scan.

* * *

```
SCAN STRUCTURE — Level 2 pill, sealed (Foundation Establishment, Founders' make)
Target: Pill (jade-domed, lacquer box)
Cost: 30 CE
CE: 37 -> 7
Note: structure of this complexity cannot be read in a single pass. Stand by.
```

It does not feel like a pass. It feels, in the pit of Jian's stomach, like falling.

A line of white light opens in the center of his vision and runs the length of the pill, from end to end, and then another, and another. The pill unfolds. It is a sphere that is also a lattice, a lattice that is also a spiral, and the spiral is made of layers, and the layers are made of threads so fine that they have no width at all. He sees the way the heat moved through it. He sees the way the Qi was folded into it, again and again, like a sheet of metal beaten into a blade.

He sees the place where, six hundred years ago, a man stopped and wept.

That is not in the panel. It is only a shape. A little knot of discontinuity at the core, the place where the maker's hand had faltered and been corrected. The pill is perfect, and it is the perfection of a thing that has been mended.

The panel returns.

```
RECONSTRUCTION COMPLETE
Item: Foundation Establishment Pill (Level 2), peak quality
Formula recovered: 5 reagents, 1 fire sequence (9 stages), 1 resonance step.
Reagents:
1. Earthheart root, 1 (Level 2, mature)
2. Azure dew, 3 drops (Level 2, Sect-restricted)
3. Second-rank beast marrow, 1 vial (Foundation-grade beast)
4. Pale jade powder, 1 liang (Level 2)
5. Sun-forged cinnabar, 2 grains (Level 2, Sect-restricted)
Fire: 9 stages, one night, steady middle.
Resonance step: not reproducible by hand at current craft limit.
Synthesis (Interface): requires all 5 reagents + approx. 150 CE.
Hand-brewing: not possible (craft limit Rank 1; Level 2 low-grade exceptional only; this formula exceeds it).
```

He reads the panel once. He reads it again, so that every line goes down into the memory he keeps for such things, the part of him that was an engineer in another life and still thinks in specifications.

Five.

The public scroll listed four. The fifth, the marrow of a beast of the second rank, is the one that was cut from the page.

And hand-brewing is out of the question. He is a QR9 with a Rank 1 craft limit. The Interface's Synthesis is the only road. One hundred and fifty points of cultivation energy, and he has seven.

I will have to earn the rest.

He closes the panel. His body has not moved. His hands, folded in front of him, have gone cold to the wrists, and a slight sweat has started at the back of his neck. He breathes in through his nose, steadily, as he was taught in the Garden, and he feels, very faintly, the Veil turn.

He keeps looking at the pill, as a boy would who was doing as he was told.

* * *

"Lin Jian."

The Elder's voice is quite pleasant.

"Yes, Elder."

"You were very still."

"I was looking, Elder."

"Mm." Bai has put down the bowl. The pale small eyes rest on him with their usual directness. "What did you see?"

Careful.

Jian turns the question over, once, with great attention. There are three possible answers. The first is nothing, which will not be believed. The second is a pill, which will not be tolerated. The third is a small true observation, one he can afford to give.

"A knot, Elder."

"A knot."

"At the center. Where the layers meet. It looks as though the maker's hand slipped, and he made it again."

The room has gone entirely quiet.

Hua Ning has taken half a step back. The young man with the long jaw is frowning. Steward Gu, by the wall, has gone as still as a post, and his small bright eyes have fixed on the floor with the fierce attention of a man who does not wish to have been seen listening.

Bai sits perfectly motionless.

"There is no knot in that pill," he says, finally.

"No, Elder?"

"The Founders made it. They did not slip." He rises. His round pink face has lost its geniality; it has become, in an instant, the face of an old man who has seen too much. "You may be mistaken. The light is poor. You may have seen a reflection in the jade."

"Yes, Elder," says Jian. "I may have."

For three breaths nothing moves. A cinder pops in the furnace.

Then Bai leans forward, slowly, till his nose is a hand's width from Jian's collar, and breathes in.

"Hm," he says.

"Elder?"

"You smell of copper." The pale eyes narrow. "Hot copper. As after a lightning strike." He straightens. "Gu."

"Elder?"

"Open the vent."

The steward scrambles. A shutter in the dome slides back, and a thin cool draft of morning air runs through the room, scattering the smoke. Jian does not exhale until it has passed.

"Furnace room," says Bai, sourly, to the apprentices. "Always a smell of something. I should have the flue cleaned." He gestures at the box. "Gu, close it. The lecture is over. You are dismissed, all of you. Except you."

He points at Jian.

* * *

When the others have gone, he does not sit.

He closes the lid of the box with his own hands, and lowers the jade dome over it, and takes up a brass key from a ring at his belt. It is a very ordinary key. He turns it twice in a lock Jian has not noticed, in the base of the stone ring, and a faint white light runs once around the circle and goes out.

"A seal," he says, to the stone. "It is not for thieves. It is for me."

"Elder."

"I have lied to you twice." Bai keeps his back turned. "Once about the knot. There is a knot. I have looked at it every year for fifty-two years, and I have never told anyone, and a youth of twenty has told me about it in front of eleven apprentices." He turns. "How did you know?"

Jian lifts his eyes. He holds the old man's gaze. He thinks of eight possible answers, and discards seven of them.

"I do not know, Elder. It was there."

"It was there."

"Yes."

"And the second lie. Do you know what it was?"

"No, Elder."

"I said you smelled of copper." The Elder's voice is very low. "I have smelled that smell once before in my life. Seventy years ago. In a boy I was apprenticed with. A boy who could see inside things."

The furnace ticks. A bead of sweat runs down Jian's spine.

"What happened to him?"

"He was very good," says Bai. "He made a pill that no one else could make. He made it for the Sect. He did not live to twenty." He picks up a plum from the bowl, looks at it, and puts it down. "I am telling you this for the second time today, Lin Jian: there is a thing the Sect is afraid of, and I have just watched it stand at my furnace and be polite."

"I am not..."

"Do not tell me what you are not." The old man waves a hand. "I do not want to know. If I do not know, I cannot be asked." He sits down heavily on the stool. "You will go and sweep the herb store. You will say nothing to anyone, about the knot, or the smell, or the lecture. Nor will I."

"Yes, Elder."

"And Lin Jian."

"Yes?"

"Whatever you saw in that pill," says Bai, not looking at him, "I hope it was worth it."

* * *

Hua Ning is waiting for him in the passage outside.

She has stationed herself against the wall beside the herb-store door, with her arms folded and her inky fingers tucked into her sleeves. The long-jawed young man, whom Jian has learned is called Cai, stands a pace behind her and looks at the ceiling.

"A knot," she says.

"Senior Sister."

"You told the Elder there was a knot in the Founders' pill." Her voice is low and level. "Three years I have stood at that ring. Cai has stood at it five. Not one of us has seen a thing but the pill." She takes a step toward him. "You have been here for six days."

"I looked at it for a long time, Senior Sister. Nobody had asked me to look before."

"That is not an answer."

"It is the only one I have."

For a moment he thinks she will strike him. Her fist closes in her sleeve. Then something in her face gives way, not into kindness, but into the tired, thin, hungry look of someone who has been working for a thing a very long time and has watched a child walk past her.

"He sent us out," she says. "He has never sent us out. He sat there with his plums, and he sent us out, and he kept you." A short breath. "I am not stupid. I know what that means. I know what you are to him."

"I do not know what I am to him."

"A reason," says Hua Ning. "He has been looking for a reason for fifty years. You are it."

She turns and goes. Cai hesitates, looks at Jian with something close to apology, and follows her down the passage.

Jian stands with his back to the wall.

A reason. It is not what he would have said. But it fits, he thinks, closer than he likes, and he carries it into the herb store along with the broom.

* * *

The herb store is cool and dim and smells of dried roots and old paper.

Jian sweeps. It is the work he was told to do, and he does it exactly, long strokes down the center aisle, short ones under the racks, a pause at the corners. A sleepy guard dozes on a stool by the door. Dust hangs in a slant of light from a high window. He is a twenty-year-old with a broom, and his hands are still cold.

Seven.

It is the number that matters. He has spent his energy on a formula, and the formula says he needs a hundred and fifty more. There is no regeneration. The Interface gives CE only for things it counts as achievements: kills of marked targets, discoveries, completed tasks. In seven months he has earned just over three hundred, and nearly all of it from a handful of single events.

The gap is the whole problem.

He sweeps. In his head, a plan assembles, as plans do, out of the pieces available. He lays it out the way he once laid out a build schedule: dependencies first, risks second, the thing that cannot be bought last. Each reagent is a task. Each task has an owner, a price and a person who will notice if it goes missing. Medicine Valley holds the root. The auction house in the market town holds the powder, if a boy ever has stones. The marrow has a heartbeat. The restricted pair have a lock on them, and keys he cannot yet name. The ledger under his cot will need a second page.

Five reagents. The root is a Level 2 herb, rare but not forbidden; the Sect's Medicine Valley grows it under guard. The jade powder can be bought, if a boy has stones, which he does not. The marrow has to come from a second-rank beast, and he is a QR9 with a pangolin who is still asleep for another twelve days.

The dew and the cinnabar are restricted. That is the line that worries him. The Sect keeps those under seal, by Elders' permission or by rank. He does not yet know which.

And the energy. A hundred and forty-three.

He stops sweeping.

Something has changed in the room. It is nothing a Mirror would catch, and nothing a Foundation cultivator on the far side of a wall would hear. It is a small dry warmth, a faint pressure behind the eyes, as of a thing clearing its throat.

A new line has formed in the corner of his vision, thin and white and faintly cold. It was not there a minute ago.

```
NOTICE — Interface status
Pending integration: Cradle (scanner coil), recovered.
Synthesis ceiling will change on cradle integration.
Recommended action: integrate at an authorized dock.
Warning: integration is irreversible.
```

The dock.

He leans on the broom. He looks at the dust in the light, for a long time, without seeing it.

At the far end of the store, the guard stirs, and yawns, and goes back to sleep.

In the furnace room behind the wall, a stout old man in a stained robe sits beside a locked stone ring and stares at the place where a boy has stood, and does not eat his plum.
